related_questions.question: What is the current U.S. immigration policy?

text_blocks.snippet: Current US immigration policy is primarily governed by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), which sets annual limits on permanent immigration and allows for various pathways for both permanent and temporary residency. The policy has two main aspects: facilitating legal immigration and focusing on immigration enforcement and removal.
snippet_highlighted_words: primarily governed by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), which sets annual limits on permanent immigration and allows for various pathways for both permanent and temporary residency

list.title: Permanent Visas:
list.snippet: The INA sets an annual limit of 675,000 permanent immigrant visas, with categories for family-sponsored, employment-based, and diversity immigrants.

list.title: Family-Sponsored:
list.snippet: Includes immediate relatives of U.S. citizens (spouses, parents, and children under 21), who are exempt from the annual numerical limits.

list.title: Employment-Based:
list.snippet: Visas are available for individuals with certain skills or job offers.

list.title: Diversity Visa Lottery:
list.snippet: A lottery system selects individuals from countries with historically low rates of immigration to the U.S.

list.title: Temporary Visas:
list.snippet: Various nonimmigrant visas allow individuals to enter the U.S. for specific purposes and durations, such as tourism, work, or study.

list.title: Refugees and Asylees:
list.snippet: The U.S. admits refugees through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program, with annual numbers determined by the President in consultation with Congress. Asylum is granted on a case-by-case basis to individuals who demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution.

list.title: Border Security:
list.snippet: Focuses on preventing unauthorized border crossings and intercepting contraband.

list.title: Interior Enforcement:
list.snippet: Includes immigration enforcement activities such as detention, deportation, and worksite enforcement.

list.title: Recent Changes:
list.snippet: The "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" (OBBBA) recently introduced new and increased fees for humanitarian-based applications and employment authorizations, according to Ogletree.com.

list.title: Executive Authority:
list.snippet: The executive branch has the power to allow certain noncitizens to enter or remain in the U.S. on a time-limited basis, through mechanisms like Temporary Protected Status (TPS) and immigration parole.

list.title: State and Local Roles:
list.snippet: States and localities play a role in immigration policy, particularly in areas like healthcare and social services.

list.title: International Cooperation:
list.snippet: U.S. immigration policy often involves international cooperation, particularly with countries that are major sources of immigration or transit countries.
The Department of Homeland Security terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti, encouraging Haitians to obtain lawful status, according to USCIS.
The U.S. has shortened the validity of non-immigrant visas for citizens of several African countries.
Changes to healthcare access for immigrants include new restrictions on Medicaid, Medicare, and Affordable Care Act Marketplace coverage for certain lawful permanent residents, notes KFF.
